headline: Nigeria Puts A One-Year Award Clock On Flare-Gas Projects
deck: The regulator’s warning turns awarded flare-site rights into a build-or-lose test, but the record still does not show one common permit deadline for every project.
body: Nigeria's upstream regulator has put a one-year review clock on flare-gas commercialization awards, with revocation available when progress is inadequate. Reuters reported the warning from a ministerial briefing, attributing the figures and threat to Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, chief executive of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission. A later sensor finding from NUPRC's own site says the regulator identified 43 flare sites, awarded 27 of them, and reviews each flare-site award one year after grant. [E1] [E2]

That clock changes the project from a policy promise into a hardware schedule. A flare site can only become saleable energy or feedstock if the holder gets access, installs compression and processing equipment, connects buyers or power users, and finances the work before the award starts to look warehoused. NUPRC's bidder material says permit holders are monitored against development milestones and schedules, and lists LNG, LPG, methanol or ammonia, and gas-to-liquids among technologies for using flare gas. [E3]

The record does not establish a single common deadline for all 27 awarded sites. The regulator's one-year language refers to review after award, and the sensor notes that NUPRC did not reconcile the 43-site and 27-award figures with earlier 49-site and 42-bidder counts. The safer reading is project by project: award dates, site access, equipment orders, offtake contracts, financing and milestone letters matter more than a single national anniversary. [E2] [E3]

A stronger reading is that Nigeria is now using revocation risk to force real buildout from companies that won flare-gas rights. The softer reading is that the warning is a public nudge until a dated revocation notice or published milestone failure shows enforcement. The fact that would decide between those readings is plain: a named award withdrawn after its one-year review, or a site-by-site schedule showing which award missed which required milestone. [E2] [E3]

Industrial upside is bounded by the same missing project data. Reuters' record says successful projects would convert otherwise burned associated gas into saleable fuel or feedstock, while NUPRC's own news item says Nigeria has more than 215 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves. Those numbers make the gas argument large, but they do not say how much flare gas the awarded sites can capture or how quickly any plant can deliver volumes. [E1] [E2]

For now, the hard count is 43 identified flare sites, 27 awards, and a one-year progress review backed by a revocation threat. That is enough to mark a build-or-lose clock, not enough to mark capacity as built. The next real movement is not another statement; it is a permit pulled, a compressor delivered, an offtake signed, or a finance close tied to one of the awarded flare sites. [E2] [E3]

evidence_box.fragment: Reuters reported from a ministerial briefing that NUPRC warned flare-gas investors they could lose permits, with Eyesan saying 27 of 43 identified flare sites had been awarded and that successful projects would convert burned associated gas into saleable fuel or feedstock.
NUPRC says it reviews each flare-site award one year after grant and may revoke it for insufficient progress; 43 sites were originally identified, 27 awarded, and proven gas reserves exceed 215 TCF.
